name: Czech
variety: Standard Czech as spoken in Bohemia (Prague); Moravian differences are noted where they matter
sources: Dankovičová, Jana (1999). Czech. In Handbook of the International Phonetic Association, 70-73. Cambridge University Press.
Šimáčková, Šárka; Podlipský, Václav Jonáš & Chládková, Kateřina (2012). Czech spoken in Bohemia and Moravia. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 42(2), 225-232.
Palková, Zdena (1994). Fonetika a fonologie češtiny. Praha: Karolinum.
Skarnitzl, Radek; Šturm, Pavel & Volín, Jan (2016). Zvuková báze řečové komunikace: Fonetický a fonologický popis řeči. Praha: Karolinum.
Skarnitzl, Radek & Volín, Jan (2012). Referenční hodnoty vokalických formantů pro mladé dospělé mluvčí standardní češtiny. Akustické listy 18.
Podlipský, Václav Jonáš; Skarnitzl, Radek & Volín, Jan (2009). High front vowels in Czech: a contrast in quantity or quality? Proceedings of Interspeech 2009.
Dankovičová, Jana & Dellwo, Volker (2007). Czech speech rhythm and the rhythm class hypothesis. Proceedings of the 16th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Saarbrücken.
Palková, Zdena & Volín, Jan (2003). The role of F0 contours in determining foot boundaries in Czech. Proceedings of the 15th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences, Barcelona.
Short, David (1993). Czech. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
contrasts: phonemic vowel length in all five vowel qualities, independent of stress (dráha [ˈdraːɦa] 'track' vs drahá [ˈdraɦaː] 'dear', byt vs být)
plain trill /r/ versus raised fricative trill /r̝/ (ř), as in řeka, moře, tři
palatal stops and nasal /c ɟ ɲ/ versus alveolar /t d n/
voiced versus voiceless obstruents, including voiced glottal /ɦ/ paired with voiceless velar /x/
syllabic /r̩ l̩/ as syllable nuclei (krk, vlk, prst, Plzeň), marginally syllabic m (sedm, osm)
allophony: /r̝/ is voiceless [r̝̊] next to a voiceless consonant, before or after it, and word-finally (tři, při, křeslo, chřipka, hořký, kuřte, keř, lékař)
word-final obstruents are devoiced before a pause and before voiceless sounds (led [lɛt], zub [zup], lev [lɛf], muž [muʃ])

obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member (kdo [ɡdo], sbor [zbor], vstát [fstaːt], tužka [ˈtuʃka], lehký [ˈlɛxkiː]), also between a non-syllabic preposition and its host (v Praze [f praze], s bratrem [z bratrɛm], k domu [ɡ domu])
/v/ is devoiced but does not voice a preceding consonant (tvůj [tvuːj]); /ɦ/ and /x/ form a voicing pair; sh is [sx] in Bohemia and [zɦ] in Moravia (shoda)
in Bohemian speech word-final obstruents stay voiceless before a sonorant or vowel of the next word (dub roste [dup rostɛ]); Moravian speech voices them
a glottal stop is usual before a word-initial vowel, especially after a pause or a preposition (v okně [f ʔokɲɛ]); it blocks voicing of the preceding consonant

short /ɪ/ is clearly lower and more central than long /iː/ in Bohemia; the other short-long pairs have nearly the same quality, with long /uː/ and /oː/ slightly more peripheral. In Moravia /ɪ/ is close to [i]
/n/ is [ŋ] before velars (banka); /m/ is [ɱ] before /f v/; /x/ has the voiced allophone [ɣ] before voiced obstruents
the letter ě after labials stands for [jɛ], after m for [ɲɛ] (město [ˈmɲɛsto])
/ɛ/ is open-mid; /a/ is central; /oː/ occurs mostly in loanwords
syllable_structure: (C)(C)(C)(C)V(C)(C)(C), with syllabic r, l (and m) as possible nuclei
phonotactics: rich onset clusters (vzhled, pstruh, čtvrt); words without any vowel are possible (krk, prst, vlk, smrt, čtvrt)
no voiced obstruents before a pause
diphthong /ou̯/ is native; /au̯/ and /ɛu̯/ occur in loanwords and interjections
geminates only at morpheme boundaries and usually simplified

stress.rule: Stress falls on the first syllable of the word; a monosyllabic preposition takes the stress from the following word (na stole [ˈna stolɛ]); clitics are unstressed.
stress.cues: weak and not marked by duration or vowel quality; mainly a pitch change, often a low stressed syllable followed by a higher post-stress syllable in Bohemian speech, with slight intensity

rhythm.notes: Traditionally called syllable-timed (no reduction, weak fixed stress); Dankovičová & Dellwo (2007) found that rhythm measures place Czech between the classes, because of complex consonant clusters and phonemic vowel length.

length.notes: Long vowels are roughly one and a half to two times as long as short ones. The duration difference is smallest for /ɪ/ vs /iː/ in Bohemian speech, where vowel quality carries much of the contrast (Podlipský, Skarnitzl & Volín 2009). Length is independent of stress, and unstressed long vowels are common.

intonation.declarative: stress groups begin low on the stressed syllable and rise on the following syllable; the final stress group falls to low (concluding cadence)
intonation.yes_no_question: rising or rise-fall contour on the last stress group: low stressed syllable, then a rise that may fall again on the last syllable of longer groups; word order need not change
intonation.wh_question: falling, like a statement, with a high question word
intonation.continuation: slight rise or high level at the end of a non-final phrase (half-cadence)
intonation.accent_shape: L*+H: low on the stressed syllable with the rise on the post-stress syllable
intonation.notes: The post-stress rise is described by Palková & Volín (2003) and is typical of Bohemian Czech.

tone.notes: No lexical tone or pitch accent.

phonation: glottal stop or creak before word-initial vowels

problems: Words whose only syllable nucleus is a syllabic l are spelled out letter by letter (vlk, pln, plch); syllabic l works when the word also has a vowel (vlna, Plzeň, slza) and syllabic r always works (krk, prst).
ř is voiceless only after p, t, k, f. It stays voiced word-finally (keř, lékař, tvář, věř), before a voiceless consonant (hořký, kuřte, mateřský) and after ch (chřipka), where Czech has [r̝̊].
k is never voiced before a voiced obstruent (kdo, kde, kdy give [kd], leckdo [d͡zkd]) and h is not devoiced to [x] before a voiceless consonant (lehký [hk]).
Final v is not devoiced (lev, krev end in [v]).
Non-syllabic prepositions are not assimilated to the next word: v Praze keeps [v], s bratrem and s dětmi keep [s], k domu keeps [k], and z domu is devoiced to [s].
Word-final obstruents stay voiced before a word beginning with a vowel or sonorant (dub roste with [b], nad oknem with [d]): this is the Moravian and Slovak pattern, not the Bohemian standard.
No glottal stop before word-initial vowels.
Stress is given the usual eSpeak marking (higher pitch and amplitude on the first syllable); the low stressed syllable with a post-stress rise is not modelled.
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
The nominal long to short vowel length in the phoneme table is about 2.4 to 1 (290 vs 120), more than the ratios reported for Czech.
good: initial stress, with monosyllabic prepositions joined to the next word and stressed (nad oknem, bez tebe, pod stolem)
phonemic vowel length from the spelling (á, é, í, ó, ú, ů, ý)
short /ɪ/ and long /iː/ use different vowel qualities
ř is a separate fricative trill phoneme with a voiceless variant
final devoicing of b, d, ď, g, h, z, ž and regressive voicing assimilation inside words (sbor, vstát, tužka, hezký)
palatal stops and ɲ, including the ě rules (město [mɲɛsto], děti [ɟɛcɪ]) and exception lists for di, ti, ni in loanwords
[ŋ] before velars; diphthongs ou, au, eu

notes: No formant or VOT values are given: reference formant values exist (Skarnitzl & Volín 2012) but I cannot quote the figures with confidence.
